entry.title: Messing up and having fun.
entry.content:
Every now and then, not often, but it happens, I mess things up. Say I've personally promised someone, "Let's meet up," and I jot it down only in my own private schedule. If I forget to report it to K, the god of my calendar, the result is always some not so small inconvenience for everyone involved. And since these promises tend to be for the evening, I sometimes end up eating dinner twice, two suppers in one night. But let's set that aside for now.

・

When I started a project called Shigesato Itoi's Live Reading, it turned out to be two solid hours of reading aloud and sharing impressions, nonstop talking that left me utterly exhausted in body and spirit. And yet, somehow, I found myself strangely enjoying it. I'd decided to do one trial run, then one proper first session, and if it seemed impossible I could just quit. But even if it is impossible, I came away wanting to do the next one.

If I do say so myself, the book selection was excellent. Naoya Shiga's The Shopboy's God, Osamu Dazai's Click-Clack Mountain, both so wonderful as fiction that they're deeply rewarding to read. What made the "Live Reading" so enjoyable was, first and foremost, that the stories themselves were wonderful. For the first time in ages, I remembered the simple pleasure of just reading a novel, not some book of theory or argument, but pure fiction. It's a joy to read, and I get to share that joy with everyone. There's no more delightful work than that, exhausting or not.

And so I've already started wanting to decide what the book for the third session will be. I've thought of some candidates, and I've begun reading a few of them. "Oh, this is lovely, this is wonderful," I think, feeling like a high school kid again. "Thank you so much for writing this," I find myself wanting to say, almost moved to express my gratitude. I'll definitely do the third session, so please look forward to it.

With all that in mind, and to prepare for any sudden karaoke, I just whipped up a batch of homemade throat remedy. I made it in a snap, poured it into a bottle, and stashed it in the fridge. All in all, I'd say my days aren't half bad.

◆Today's question is no.064: "By the way, are you healthy?"

Either way, if you'd like, drop me an email and let me know.

Thanks again for coming to Hobonichi today. What you eat, what you sing, these things matter too.
entry.summary: The author discovers renewed joy in reading and sharing great fiction aloud through his "Live Reading" project, finding that the simple pleasure of experiencing wonderful stories—and sharing that experience with others—makes even exhausting work deeply rewarding.

entry.title: Good times, good people, good things.
entry.content:
The third floor of Hobonichi in Kanda is built, if I had to describe it, like a family restaurant. It doesn't matter who's standing or sitting where. Working, chatting, eating, debating, dozing off, none of it draws any complaint as long as it isn't a serious nuisance to others. There are other, quieter floors, so you can just move if you want to. You're free to peer over someone's shoulder or from the side while they work, hold a meeting, or show something off, and in a sense, some meetings are held precisely because people want to be peered at. This is also the floor where snacks people have given us and all sorts of delicious things get lined up on the counter with a cheerful "Help yourselves." We designed it from the very start to be that kind of place.

During so-called working hours, putting on a so-called working face and staring seriously at a computer screen matters far less than talking about chess, which someone's recently gotten into, or recounting the shock of watching "We Are Aliens," or wondering aloud whether a certain Chinese restaurant's summer-only "chilled scallion noodles" has gone back to being shrimp fried rice now that it's October. Thinking and talking about things like that is what's important. Incidentally, I can't eat shrimp, I'm allergic.

The labor and time spent drafting throwaway plans E, F, and G just to show your counterpart the process of effort you've put in. The hours spent pretending to work diligently. Things like that aren't merely a waste, they're an active hindrance. Far more valuable is the time spent talking back and forth, like a bunch of middle schoolers, about what's fun, what's delightful, what's sad, what's lonely. Everyone already does the serious, steady grind. I think the hours of forced "pretending to work" would be better turned into enjoyable play, for the person's own health, for the mood of their colleagues, and for the future of humanity.

◆Today's question is no. 063: "What is a good time, for you?" Give it some thought, and if you feel like it, let us know by email.

Thank you, as always, for coming to Hobonichi today. People from outside sometimes say, "Hobonichi is actually pretty strict, you know."
entry.summary: Hobonichi's third floor is intentionally designed as a relaxed, family-restaurant-like space where genuine human connection, playful conversation, and creative thinking are valued far more than the performative appearance of productivity. The author argues that this culture of allowing people to be authentically themselves—rather than pretending to work—ultimately benefits individual wellbeing, team morale, and creative output.

entry.title: Meeting by chance and simply talking.
entry.content:
I've probably had more chances than most people to meet others and talk with them. Some I know well, some I know only a little, and sometimes I meet people I hardly know at all. It's not as if I show up having done zero research on them, zero thought about what we might talk about. That would be too much. But I make a point of not "researching thoroughly" or "preparing carefully."

If someone wants to prepare for something "thoroughly," by all means, go ahead. On one condition, though: that they're ready to let all that enormous preparation go to waste.

Map out the route too precisely and it's guaranteed to be no fun. When two people meet, it's the moment a kind of "living thing" is born. If both sides just take turns reciting things they already know perfectly well, it's hard for anything to come of it, and honestly, the conversation itself isn't interesting while it's happening. You might come away thinking you "learned something," sure. But I think what's most interesting is when both people stumble onto some small new discovery together.

I once explained this way of meeting people to the other person directly. I was about to have a conversation with someone from overseas whom I'd never met, and I started by saying, "Shall we talk like two strangers who just happened to end up sitting next to each other at a bar?" Even with a bit of prior knowledge, asking "So, where are you from?" all over again is exactly the sort of thing a neighbor at a bar might do. I've kept doing this kind of thing over and over, and it's made me who I am today.

That said, this thing I'm writing here, the former "Today's Darling," who exactly am I writing it for, and what am I actually doing? Maybe it's like the owner of some little shop making small talk with a customer from down the street, going, "Seems like there's a lot of pollen in the air lately, huh..." Which kind of roasted sweet potato is the tastiest, a good manga I came across, and sometimes, with a perfectly straight face, something solemn and self-important too.

◆Today's question is no. 062: "Anything good happen to you lately?" Whether something did or didn't, it's all just small talk. Let me know by email.

Thank you, as always, for stopping by Hobonichi today.

When things don't go the way you wanted, maybe it's that "the way you wanted" was the questionable part.
entry.summary: The author argues that meaningful human connection comes from approaching conversations with openness and minimal preparation, allowing genuine discoveries to emerge organically rather than simply exchanging pre-planned information.

entry.title: Some thoughts I had over the weekend
entry.content:
So the Hanshin Tigers clinched the pennant, and with that, the baseball season has finally wrapped up. What a season it was. All sorts of things happened. The Giants' manager suddenly stepped down one day, and the man who was told, "You take over," well, that's no small thing to be handed. You can't exactly sit back and say something modest like, "Oh, someone like me couldn't possibly..." Not when it's professional baseball, where "fighting spirit" is the whole point. It must have been rough. In a way, it was a year of rebuilding. Day after day, it was about rising up from a tough position and figuring out how to see the fight through to the end. And to still be in the running for the title late in the season, I'd say that's more than enough to be proud of. Of course, if you start wanting more, there's no end to it.

I went to see "We Are Aliens" for the second time. I almost never used to watch a movie more than once, but maybe "Chiikawa" got me into the habit. Maybe I just want to take in all that painstaking handiwork, the way you can tell the people who made it went to such lengths, right down to the smallest details. And the second viewing was good again. It really is something. The enthusiasm, the care, the sense of taste, all of it is left behind as expression in every corner of the film. Maybe going to see it again felt like going on a hunt to discover all of that. Like spotting an ammonite fossil in a marble wall. And let me tell you, this movie is absolutely crawling with ammonites. And in a larger sense, I think it's a story of "affirmation." Remember how there used to be a movie tagline that went, "Live."? I almost want to borrow it again right here. That's the feeling it left me with. By the final scene, I actually ended up in tears.

People are free to think whatever they think, and to say whatever they say. But because they're free, they also end up thinking and saying cruel things. Once, something like that would have been born and vanished like a bubble, tucked away in some corner where no one would ever see it. But these days, even graffiti in a back alley is a form of transmission that other people can see. Lies, slander, foul-mouthed insults, they all go flying off into the air. And without even realizing it, we breathe them in too.

◆Today's question is no. 061: "What would you write on a blank sheet of paper?" So, what would it be? If you'd like, feel free to send us an email.

Thank you, as always, for stopping by Hobonichi today. Kyoto, Shibuya PARCO, Akagi, Kanda, everyone's doing well.
entry.summary: The essay reflects on the beauty of craftsmanship and intentional creation—whether in cinema or sports—while grappling with how modern technology amplifies both human connection and cruelty in ways that feel inescapable.

entry.title: The festival's over, and I'm not even sad.
entry.content:
It won't make the news anywhere, being the kind of purely local affair that it is, but yesterday, at the "Kanda Nishikicho Ennichi" festival, our team, the "Hobonichi Hipparees," won the "Tug-of-War Tournament 2026," reclaiming the trophy we'd once crafted ourselves out of prize money from years past. Who knew a victory after three long years could feel this good? The Hobonichi crowd was positively choked up with tears of joy.

Truly, it's a bit of local news, a shameless bit of self-promotion, the result of a competition that may well strike some as trivial. But for the neighbors of Kanda Nishikicho in Chiyoda Ward, it was a "festival" that had everyone fired up for the first time in ages.

Now, Kanda has always had the "Kanda Matsuri," a grand festival known all across the country. There's no payment for the labor, of course, and come to think of it, no trophy to fight over either, and the preparations that come around once every two years are an enormous, exhausting undertaking. And yet, "We do it." Because this is Kanda.

It all started, really, back when our company was first set to move to this neighborhood. The elders of the local association pressed us firmly on one point: "You'll be taking part in the festival, won't you?" W-well, of course we'll take part! It's an absolute blast, after all.

But, aside from the "Kanda Matsuri," there also turned out to be this thing called the "Kanda Nishikicho Ennichi," and that one caught us completely off guard. Still, "We do it!" Because that's just how Nishikicho is.

Four years ago, we didn't just set up our signature "Twice-the-Fun Yo-Yo Fishing" stall, so very Hobonichi. We also threw ourselves into the "Tug-of-War Tournament" with a cry of, "Let's take this seriously!" And so, Hobonichi, a company that usually acts like a bunch of goof-offs who skip club activities to head straight home, gritted its teeth and actually went and won the whole thing. Which got everyone in town going, "Oh yeah? Then so will we!" They caught fire too. These things are always more fun the more seriously you take them.

And so, this year, 2026, the number of participating teams swelled to 48. The venue moved to a larger spot, and by the neighborhood association chairman's eyeball estimate, the crowd of spectators and participants, young and old, men and women alike, came to "around 5,000." A roaring success. A festival that brings neither profit nor loss, offering, for this one night only, the thrill of winning and losing. Honestly, "having a neighborhood" really is a wonderful thing, isn't it?

◆ Today's question is no. 060: "When you hear the word 'festival,' what comes to mind?"

Give it some thought, and if you feel like it, send your answer to me by email.

Thank you, as always, for visiting Hobonichi today. The Hobonichi crew, believe it or not, actually gets plenty of real work done too.
entry.summary: A local company's tug-of-war victory reignites community spirit in their Tokyo neighborhood, demonstrating how taking small, local traditions seriously can transform a modest festival into a unifying celebration that brings thousands together.

entry.title: Wandering about, another day just like any other.
entry.content:
Yesterday, in something of a muddle, I wrote that October 1st was going to be "quite a day," and somehow or other I made it through. Most of the days I'd dreaded, the ones where I kept thinking "I'm scared of when this day comes," end up becoming "yesterday" one way or another. That's just how it goes. "Shigesato Itoi's Live Reading" really was hard work, but it was the kind of hard work that felt genuinely worthwhile. Above all, I enjoyed it myself. I suppose what I'm doing is simply taking what I normally do silently, alone, in my head, and letting myself have fun with it out loud. I probably won't stop just yet. I'm thinking about a third book.

I'd left my smartphone behind and was out when I suddenly remembered something I absolutely had to get in touch about. If I went home or back to the office it would sort itself out, but I couldn't wait that long, so I was getting a little frantic. Wasn't there one of those old red public phones somewhere? I looked, but of course there was no such thing. And yet, by some stroke of luck, there was a phone booth. Surely the phone inside wouldn't have been removed? Oh good, it was fine, there it was, an actual phone. No phone card in my wallet, but I had a ten-yen coin. All I had to do was make the call, and up to that point everything was fine. But then it hit me. I didn't know the number. If it's saved in your phone, you can call without knowing the number at all. Of course. I never knew the numbers in the first place. And yet somehow I used to make calls, used to send messages and all the rest. Come to think of it, the only phone number I have memorized these days is my home number, the one you write down when applying for something. It's quite possible I don't know a single other one. The only thing that comes to mind is that old jingle, the "Castella is number one, the phone is number two" song. And even then, dialing just "two" would hardly get you through to Bunmeido.

It reminded me of the time my electric toothbrush ran out of battery, and until it finally dawned on me that I could just brush by hand, I stood there frozen, thinking, oh no, what do I do. Convenience can shade into inconvenience, I suppose, but well, there's no helping it.

◆Today's question no.059: "Looking back, how far I've come." What's yours? Feel free to think it over, and if you like, send it to us by email.

Thank you for coming to Hobonichi again today. A tug of strength against strength, technique against technique. Today is the day of the tug-of-war tournament!
entry.summary: The essay reflects on how modern conveniences like smartphones have made us dependent and forgetful—unable to remember phone numbers or function without them—while celebrating the author's own experience of performing live and sharing their creative work publicly. It explores the paradox that convenience can become its own form of inconvenience when we lose basic skills we once took for granted.

entry.title: There's nothing I can do about myself.
entry.content:
Yikes.

It's just dawned on me, October 1st is going to be a handful. I'm sitting down to write this in the middle of the night, as always, but tomorrow morning begins with the one thing I'm no good at: getting up early. I've got a CT scan scheduled, so it's off to the hospital first thing. I booked it so long ago I'd completely forgotten about it. Then in the afternoon, slotted in among the usual work, there's one of those appointments for my so-called "workout." Part of me thinks skipping it would make life easier, but no, it's the opposite. On a day like this, moving the body is probably exactly what I need. So I'll go, grumbling the whole way, and do it properly.

The real problem comes after that.

"Shigesato Itoi's Live Reading #1" was looming on the schedule.

Why on earth did I pick this day? I could ask the telephone pole, but it wouldn't know. Ask it where it lives, no answer. Ask it its name, no answer. Just a little cat, mewing to itself.

There's one precedent, so I know from experience: this takes an enormous amount of stamina and nerve. I may make it look like I'm just fluttering along, breezy and effortless, but you'd understand soon enough if you tried it yourself. The reading parts I have to do in my own voice, too, so honestly, I'm worried about whether I can even pull it off. In case you've forgotten, I'm past sixty. Day to day, I'm a doddering old man shuffling about. There'll be kanji I can't read, and my thinking isn't exactly deep either.

But then again, this whole thing was my idea in the first place, and the person in charge is that most fearsome Ms. N. So-and-so, which means there's no escaping it. Maybe I'll keep some of that powdered Ryukakusan throat remedy from the aluminum can on hand. And once we wrap the recording, maybe I'll go grab some chive soba or something. I have no idea how many hours this is going to take. A Shincho Bunko paperback, just a short story, but sixty-seven pages... oh dear.

Live on.

◆Today's question is no. 058: "Was there ever a time you wanted to run away?" If you're up for it, give it some thought and send your answer by email.

Thank you, as always, for stopping by Hobonichi today. For now, I think I'll hop in the bath nice and early and get some sleep.
entry.summary: Shigesato Itoi expresses anxiety about an unexpectedly demanding day ahead—a medical appointment, workout, and an exhausting live reading event he himself scheduled—yet resolves to push through with determination despite his age and doubts about his own capabilities.

entry.title: Again: the story of when I came in 8th place.
entry.content:
I've told this same story over and over again. It's about the days when I was completely absorbed in fishing.

There was a local bass fishing tournament held at Lake Kawaguchi. It was a regular competition, held a few times a year, and I think around 150 people usually took part. Me, a proper middle-aged man, would line up at the reception desk from around six in the morning, waiting for the start alongside younger folks and students who were all my seniors when it came to fishing. I can't remember whether the tournament ended at one in the afternoon or some other time, but the idea was that you'd have your catch weighed in turn and compete for a ranking.

As a newcomer, I was one of the older working adults, but I was one of the worse ones. I usually placed around 80th, squarely in the "thanks for participating" group. But then, one day, I had a feeling I'd actually caught a decent amount, and when I had it all weighed in and the results came out, I'd landed in 8th place.

This whole rambling piece I've written could really just come down to those two characters: "8th place."

Normally, watching sports and the like, I only ever paid attention to the battle for first. I'd feel crushed when someone lost in 2nd, or disappointed by a 5th. So when someone like me came in not first, not fifth, but 8th, I was so genuinely happy that tears actually welled up.

Eighth place is amazing, I realized. When you're not a competitor yourself, just watching the fight for the top, 8th place is something you can't even begin to think about. But once you become the one actually taking part, you understand just how happy 8th place can make you (and I suppose you'd also understand the frustration of 8th, too).

When you look at Mount Fuji, it's normal to look at the summit. But Fuji exists together with those vast, sweeping foothills too. I looked it up, and even the fifth station, where you can go by bus, is about 2,300 meters above sea level. If you were to walk all the way to the top, even the fifth station is quite something.

"Understanding that there are things you can only imagine because you're not the one involved, and then, on top of that, becoming able to imagine what it's like for the person who is." Maybe that's the kind of practice we're all doing. And yet, honestly, we still don't really understand it at all.

◆Today's question no.057: "Have you ever won an award or a prize?"

How about it? Give it some thought, and if you feel like it, send me an email.

Thank you, as always, for coming to Hobonichi today.

There are some things you just can't reach, no matter how much grit, effort, or talent you have.
entry.summary: The author discovers that achieving 8th place in a fishing tournament brings unexpected joy, revealing that genuine accomplishment and happiness aren't found only at the top, but come from participating and understanding experiences beyond what we can merely observe from the outside.

entry.title: Me in this vast world.
entry.content:
The mosquito that lands on your cheek is fiercer than any flying dragon at the edge of the earth. The wailing of your son claws at the heart more than the song of the Sirens. (from The Dead End Road)

The things that happen right around us are, for a single human being, greater than anything else. And yet, while I say this, what I'm about to talk about is no bigger than the tip of a fingernail. No, really, it is about the tips of fingernails.

For many years I lived as a devoted nail-clipper enthusiast, but for some months now I haven't touched a nail clipper at all. I just buff down whatever has grown with a glass nail file. I started it half-heartedly, telling myself I'd quit when I got bored or go back to the old way when it became a bother, but I've kept it up this whole time without stopping. Only, lately I've switched from the glass file to a pen-shaped product called the "Nail King," which is simpler and doesn't scatter the shavings. Who would have thought a day would come when I'd file down my grown nails instead of using scissors or clippers.

This next thing might seem even smaller, but at long last the announcement has gone out for "Shigesato Itoi's Live Reading."

We tried it once as a test, and it was genuinely fun. All it involves is reading a book and sharing my impressions in front of only my own colleagues, family really. What do people think about while they're reading a book? I decided to make myself the guinea pig and find out. The problem is that it will expose the fact that "I'm not thinking about anything much." I'm no scholar or expert, so I simply read. Books aren't written by logic to begin with. Reading is a person writing and a person reading, plain and simple. Most little arguments and hair-splitting come after the fact anyway. In the spirit of "life really begins once your stupidity is out in the open," I intend to do this live, as just one of the little folk.

◆Today's question is no.056, "On My Own Smallness." Give it some thought, and if you'd like, write it down in an email and send it to us.

Thank you again today for coming to Hobonichi. Do jot down the reader-interview questions and your answers for yourself, too.
entry.summary: The essay celebrates the profound significance of life's smallest, most intimate moments—from the mundane shift in how one files their nails to the simple act of reading and sharing thoughts—arguing that these everyday experiences matter far more than grand, distant concerns. Through embracing one's own ordinariness and stupidity, the author suggests we find authentic meaning in the small things that actually surround us.

entry.title: Language has always been squiggly.
entry.content:
"Chiikawa" is short for "chiisakute kawaii yatsu," a small and cute little thing. "Mirishira" is short for saying you didn't know even one millimeter's worth about something. And "tamageta," meaning to be astonished, apparently comes from the idea of your very soul vanishing.

Oh, I see, is that so, I find myself thinking. Being startled really is like having your soul slip away, isn't it. Looking into the origins of words is quite a lot of fun. A famous example is the word for twilight, "tasogare." It comes from an old phrase meaning "who is that person over there?", the hour when it grows dark and you can no longer tell one face from another. There's something rather lovely about that one too, don't you think?

"Arigatou," thank you, comes from "arigatashi," which is to say that something is difficult to have or to come by. You're grateful because someone has done for you a thing that rarely happens. These are the sorts of things I've been taught, or overheard, over the years.

But what I actually want to talk about today lies one step further back than all of this.

"Tasogare" is made up of two words, "who" and "that person." I understand that much, I can follow it that far, that's all perfectly clear. But then, where did the words for "who" and "that person" themselves come from? Where did "ari" and "katashi" originate? Around when did they first appear, and how did they take shape?

I'm aware that this kind of research exists, of course. But when you start tracing it back the way you'd follow the branches of an evolutionary tree in biology, you inevitably arrive at "well, what was there in the very beginning?", drifting toward something like the origin of life itself.

And the thing is, words didn't evolve according to some precise set of laws. They've been used and bent and misspoken and forgotten, repeating that kind of change over and over like living creatures, until they became what they are now. That's just how it works, and I find it fascinating.

A dictionary tells you what a "dog" is, but that entry is really just a provisional casebook, a record of "this is the kind of thing everyone has agreed to call a dog." Isn't there something delightful in all this bewildering messiness?

◆ Today's question is no. 055: "Where does your name come from?"

Think back on it, and if you feel like it, write it down and send it to us by email.

Thank you again today for coming to Hobonichi.

It makes me want to travel back up the flowing river, just to see where it all begins.
entry.summary: The essay celebrates the organic, messy evolution of language by tracing word origins and exploring how words continuously change and reshape themselves over time, much like living creatures. Rather than seeking definitive answers, the author finds wonder in the endless mystery of where language ultimately begins.

entry.title: On my silly recent circumstances.
entry.content:
I've been writing this "Today's Darling (as it was formerly called)" every single day, and I've never once forgotten to write it. Before I fall asleep, I make absolutely certain to finish it, and only then do I go to bed.

What's a little embarrassing to admit, though, is that I do sometimes forget to send in the piece I've written. It happens a few times a year, and I'll get a phone call in the morning. To make the eleven o'clock update, someone will say, "We haven't received your manuscript."

The thing is, the piece is right there on my desk. All that's left is to send it, so I say sorry, sorry, and fire it off immediately. Actually, when you've been doing this for over twenty-eight years, there turn out to be all sorts of patterns to forgetting to send in your work, but I'll spare you the details.

And so, well, yesterday brought a first for me: a case where the piece itself simply hadn't been written.

I had dealt with the more familiar "we haven't received it," and, thoroughly reassured, was yawning and thinking I might drift back to sleep, when a second prompt arrived, delicious as a fresh dashi poured over the first: "There's no reader interview at the end."

Ah, that might be true, yes, that was it!

Lately there have been a string of days off, and since my daytime schedule has been my own, I've been able to do things like write the next day's "Today's Darling (as it was formerly called)" while it's still light out. If I write it ahead of time, I can go about my evening and late night with room to spare, and even turn in early if I like. Wanting that sense of ease, I write it in the bright of the afternoon, and then I can relax, thinking, "I don't have to write anything more today."

Relax a little too much, and I forget to send it. That happens too. What's more, I'd left the "question" part blank, telling myself I'd think it over later at my leisure. You fool, you fool! That blank space was the true culprit.

This "reader interview" is something I set out to do one hundred times. I don't think it's fine to stop at fifty-two. And I myself find real pleasure in tossing out a question each day and receiving the answers. For just a moment I nearly thought, "Maybe I'll take today off," but no, that won't do, I told myself right away, and posted it, late.

◆Today's question is no. 054, "What would you do with 5,000 yen?" (No. 015 was 500 million yen.) Please write your answer in an email and send it to us.

Thank you, as always, for coming to Hobonichi today.

Sometimes it's only when someone asks that you finally understand something about yourself.
entry.summary: A daily columnist reflects on nearly three decades of disciplined writing habits, discovering through a rare missed deadline that external accountability and reader engagement are what truly drive her commitment to her work.

entry.title: Guided by the trailer, I watched "We Are Aliens."
entry.content:
When you go to see a single movie like Chiikawa six times, you end up watching the trailers in the theater exactly that many times. And naturally, among those trailers, you find something that catches your eye. Which is how I came to think, I want to see this, and headed out on opening day for an animated film called We Are Aliens.

Why did I want to see it? The reason was the images on the screen. No, really, I'd taken in almost no information beyond that. It was just that those visuals, the way the backgrounds and objects and characters were rendered, struck me as tremendously fresh and new.

It wasn't only realism. There was a hand-drawn touch to it too. You could call it painterly, or photographic, but it also brought to mind the manga of Taiyo Matsumoto and the like. This was not a foreign work. It was unmistakably Japan, somewhere around the Heisei era. If I lingered on the images, I found I only wanted to keep looking at them.

So I decided not to look at anything else, not the story, not the introductions or the explanations. First and foremost, it was the pictures, and the way those pictures moved looked interesting. And if the film itself turned out to be a dud, well, so be it. I made my theater reservation in something like the spirit of drawing a lottery ticket.

The title, We Are Aliens, has a vaguely science-fiction flavor to it, and it also feels almost like a parody. Having watched it, I can say this title suited the film well, though I also think it would have been plenty interesting under a different one.

I won't say too much about the content, but what it brought to my mind was Stand by Me. That said, there's none of the dry, sun-baked feel of a Lucas film. From beginning to end, whether rain or sweat or blood or river or tap water or fish tank, water is being drawn on the screen the entire time. It was a film soaked through for a solid two hours, and that in itself was remarkable.

And what it tells, in a sense, is a self-introduction. It's the self-introduction of a person called "we," spoken by the two protagonists. There will surely be viewers in the audience who sync up with it, thinking, that's me too. And that, after all, is probably exactly what the person introducing themselves was hoping for. I find myself wanting to learn more about the planning, the screenplay, the director.

◆ Oh, and today's question, no. 053: "Are you lucky?" How about it? Give it some thought and send your answer by email.

Thank you again today for coming to Hobonichi. Now that I've gotten into the habit of going to the movie theater, I've grown a lot more familiar with films.
entry.summary: The author describes being drawn to the animated film *We Are Aliens* purely by its visual style—a striking blend of painterly and photographic techniques—and discovering that its poignant story about self-introduction and connection justified their gamble on appearance alone. Through its masterful use of water imagery and resonant themes, the film demonstrates how powerful visual storytelling can create meaningful emotional connections with audiences.

entry.title: Feeling the unnecessary things
entry.content:
"To feel."

To feel something. To feel the heat, to feel the cold, to feel loneliness, to feel joy, to feel friendship, to feel affection, to feel a slight, to feel anger... There are things that nearly everyone would feel, just by being there in that moment, in that place. And there are times when you weren't really feeling much of anything, but someone else nearby is feeling it, and you get pulled along and end up feeling it too. A single person's act of feeling is complex and subtle. If I had to compare it to something, I'd call it a sense of touch.

Sometimes you feel things you didn't need to. The kind of unnecessary things that everyone else overlooks. Honestly, it might have been better not to feel them at all, and sometimes feeling them stirs up a bit of confusion. You could call it a sense of unease, that sort of thing.

And then you find yourself dwelling on that unnecessary thing for a while. Sometimes you keep thinking about it for quite a long time.

Continuing to dwell on this unnecessary thing leads you into thinking about it from all sorts of angles. And once you start turning it over in your mind, that unnecessary thing you first felt can become an entirely new perspective, a fresh way in, and the thought comes together, gets put into action, and grows into what becomes obvious to everyone in the future. Most of what we call good things happen exactly this way.

Let's try applying this idea of the unnecessary thing to all kinds of examples. Sports, creative work, business, policy. You'll find that in everything, there's this same cycle that begins with a sense of unease. Feeling the unnecessary thing, then dwelling on it, then thinking it through from every direction. Everything starts with feeling, out there in the field.

AI has no field, no daily life, so its ability to feel is weak. And whether you have too much experience or too little, your ability to feel weakens all the same.

◆Today's question, no. 052: "The sense of unease I'm feeling." What is it, I wonder? If something comes to mind, feel free to send it my way, by email or however you like.

Thank you, as always, for coming to Hobonichi today. I think I wrote something rather important here, though I wonder how it came across.
entry.summary: The essay argues that genuine innovation and progress begin with noticing and dwelling on small, seemingly unnecessary feelings of unease that others overlook, a capacity for nuanced sensing that AI and overly experienced humans alike lack. True insight emerges not from efficiency but from the patient, multifaceted exploration of these subtle emotional impressions.

entry.title: Thoughts while gazing out at the endless rain.
entry.content:
This year there seems to be an awful lot of rain. I haven't been keeping track or counting the days, but it feels like I'm worrying about rain more than in a usual summer or a usual autumn. Then again, I've said the phrase "the long rains of autumn" plenty of times before, so maybe this is just what autumn is normally like. I can't say for sure.

With the long weekend, not seeing anyone from the office and staying in because of the rain, I catch myself thinking, so this is what the life of a hermit must be like. I could just go out, rain or wind or typhoon and all. It's not as if there's nothing to do at home. There's endless things to do.

But the things you ought to do get pushed aside, and instead you find yourself wanting to knock out the things you don't need to do first. You go looking for those unnecessary things with surprising seriousness. Sometimes that means "making fried rice," or, as I've done to exhaustion in the past, "making jam."

Right now I have this thing I call "Chiikawa calligraphy practice," so whenever it occurs to me I could just do that. But once a small daily pleasure starts becoming a good habit, it gets "promoted" into something I have to do. And so I end up hunting for even more things I don't need to do.

I watch films and dramas I'd figured I could skip. The ones I've saved up thinking "I'm definitely going to watch this" I want to watch properly, so the ones I can start half-heartedly are the films I'd more or less decided I didn't really need to see. The same goes for books. When there's a book I've settled on as "this looks interesting, I'm absolutely reading it," I end up starting on some other book I'd bought almost as an afterthought beforehand.

Over the course of these long rains, there have been quite a lot of not-the-favorite dramas and books I read on a whim. I watched a fair bit of the Asian Games, too. I even took up "sudoku," which I'd never touched before. And all of them, each in its own way, you could say were interesting enough. Maybe it's the ones we don't think of as "the favorite" that we end up growing close to.

◆Today's question is no.051, "Is there something you just can't help doing?" Ask yourself, and if you like, let me know by email.

Thank you again today for coming to Hobonichi. A shortage of rain is hard, but so is rain that won't quit. Just the right amount is best!
entry.summary: During rainy days spent at home, the author discovers that the things we pursue without pressure—unnecessary hobbies, forgotten books, and casual pastimes—often prove more rewarding than the obligations we feel compelled to complete.

entry.title: (Prior text omitted) Do the fools of this floating world get up and work?
entry.content:
There are countless things Shohei Ohtani has shown the world. Listing them one by one would go on forever, so I'll leave that aside. But there's one thing that seems to have slipped past most people's notice, and so, on behalf of Japan, the small island nation that produced him, I thought I'd offer my own modest word about it.

It's this: the man sleeps well.

He's said as much himself, and the people around him say it too. Apparently his routine is to sleep ten hours a day, naps included. Here is a person accomplishing all those extraordinary things, and he sleeps ten hours.

Somehow, that makes it easier for everyone to accept. If some perfectly ordinary person announced, "I sleep ten hours a day," they'd probably get a snide "Maybe you should work a little harder." I don't know if this is unique to Japan, but generally speaking, being awake and working has always been considered the "virtuous" thing.

And the people on the other end, the "work and work and work and work" types, seem to manage it by cutting into their sleep. The logic is that there's more you can do while you're awake. That's an easy enough idea to grasp. Squeezing in a bit more practice, sparing not a moment to prepare, to study. All of it is possible precisely because you're awake, your eyes open. Even playing around, even indulging in a hobby, you do it awake. The time spent sleeping was thought of as "nothing," a blank.

But by sleeping his fill, and by treating that sleep as "precious time" that feeds into his work, Shohei Ohtani has promoted "sleep (or rest)" to the status of important time. To put it in a way I don't much like, "sleep is a cost paid toward improved productivity," and if you manage it well, it yields results. Sleep has gone from being "empty time" to being "an essential nutrient."

Isn't that a rather wonderful thing? It's not as if Ohtani is the one who proposed this theory, but the fact that he's actually "sleeping well" and doing so much is a big deal. Still, imagine being someone who can even work hard at sleeping.

◆So the question, too, is simple. No. 050: "Are you sleeping well?"

If you'd like, give it some thought and send me your answer by email.

Thank you, as always, for coming to Hobonichi today. I'm the anxious sort myself, so I stay up and end up busying myself with all kinds of things.
entry.summary: Shohei Ohtani's commitment to sleeping ten hours daily challenges the cultural assumption that productivity requires sacrificing rest, demonstrating instead that quality sleep is not wasted time but an essential investment in peak performance. Through his example, sleep has been reframed from an empty void into vital recovery time that enables extraordinary achievement.

entry.title: The image of "serious damage"
entry.content:
In a sense, it's not all that unusual, but whenever "a large and powerful typhoon approaches the Japanese archipelago," the effects are enormous. Some people suffer direct damage, and no doubt a great many others are hit indirectly. I mean the people who were planning to hold outdoor events, those who work in transportation by air, land, or sea, and then, further removed, the people connected to all of that. The catering companies, for instance, must have had a hard time of it too. And of course, the harm reaches the spectators and passengers as well.

At times like these, the news reports things like "flights cancelled," "service suspended," "event called off." Sitting in your room watching television, it's easy to take in news of a "suspension" or a "cancellation" as someone else's problem, but for the people on the ground, at the actual site, these are grave decisions, and surely a very serious matter indeed. The scale of the damage and the impact is often described in numbers, too.

I don't think it's just my imagination, but reports of natural disasters seem to have grown far more frequent. This large, powerful Typhoon No. 25, too, has been covered almost without pause, and a great many people probably know exactly where it is right now.

And in the middle of all this, something occurred to me for the first time. Things like "cancellation," "flight cancelled," or "service suspended" are indeed a serious matter for the events and the transit systems, yet they are treated as something that "can happen," something "built into the system." No one wants to do it, but it is anticipated. Even when there's a huge loss involved, cancellation is a decision that can be made. It's what people call risk management. And it struck me that large-scale examples of it turn out to be surprisingly common.

In our daily lives, we go about in fear of this or that little failure, but our society today is actually making huge judgment calls all the time. During the pandemic, too, society changed so drastically, come to think of it.

◆Today's Question 049: "What's the biggest failure of your life so far?" What could it be? If you'd like, write it down in an email and send it to us.

Thank you, as always, for visiting Hobonichi today.

The everyday "sense of loss" and the kind we reckon with in an emergency must be counted on entirely separate ledgers.
entry.summary: When major disasters force society to make massive decisions like cancelling events and suspending services, it reveals that risk management and accepting large-scale failures are already built into how our world operates, a stark contrast to the minor anxieties we fret over in daily life.

entry.title: Fried rice: my longing versus reality
entry.content:
At some point I developed an interest in fried rice, and started eating it all over the place. I used to think of it as something you had at the end of a Chinese meal, but lately I've been ordering it on its own at neighborhood Chinese joints. Just the fried rice, a little bowl of soup, maybe some pickles. I thought it might feel a bit lonely, that combination, but it doesn't. And fried rice, it seems to me, is rarely a disappointment.

Once you come to love fried rice, you start to feel a fondness for the cooks who make it so deftly. The famous flick of the wok, the fierce roar of gas flames beneath it, the eggs beaten and waiting, the meat, the scallions, all the ingredients prepped in advance, the clang and clatter of the iron ladle against the wok, the final shaping of the rice into a neat little dome, and then the shout to the server delivering the order: "Fried rice!" How could you not be filled with longing?

(omitted) So, slipping past the watchful eye of my household superior, the one who dreads the pointless accumulation of kitchen gadgets, I bought a wok by mail order. Not the iron one I'd been dreaming of, but titanium, and for the ladle I chose a bamboo spatula. Then a big bottle of rice oil. All of it different from what the pros use. The truth is, I arrived at these choices after careful consultation with AI.

I decided not to bother with cold rice either, going instead with rice that was still somewhat warm, and I resolved to resist the urge to flip the wok. I would stay an amateur and make honestly delicious fried rice. In moments like these, I am quite the earnest fellow.

One afternoon, with the kitchen chief away, I sprang into action. "Now's my chance." Wait, do I have the ingredients? Scallions, yes. There's pork too, but I'll go with bacon. Eggs, check. And some good rice in the freezer. Pepper, salt, a bit of kombu seasoning. This will work, I was sure of it.

By now I understood the concept completely. Fried rice is simply egg-over-rice, stir-fried. Add some aromatics and a few ingredients to that, and there's no way it could turn out bad. The titanium wok, the warmish rice, the bamboo spatula, all of it worked out fine. Next time it'll be ramen-style fried rice, with roast pork, bamboo shoots, and scallions. This Silver Week is turning out to be rather fun.

◆Today's question, number 048: "What dish would you like to try making?" Give it some thought, and if you'd like, send us an email.

Thank you, as always, for coming to Hobonichi today.

When I choose substance over style, that's when you know I'm serious.
entry.summary: A home cook discovers genuine joy in mastering the simple art of fried rice, finding that pursuing humble culinary pleasures with earnest effort—rather than professional perfectionism—yields both delicious results and unexpected satisfaction.

entry.title: Shibuya Seibu will be gone next month.
entry.content:
I decided to go to the Shibuya Seibu to buy some Turkish sweets made with pistachio. Really, I was using that as an excuse. I wanted to see the Shibuya Seibu one more time before it closed. I'd had a vague sense that it would be gone sometime this autumn, but only then did I learn the actual date: Wednesday, September 30th. It might well have vanished without my even noticing. Somewhere along the way, it had quietly become that sort of thing to me.

I did a little shopping, wandered across a few floors, took in the corridors and walls and stairways, and tried to savor the sort of commonplace sentimentality you'd expect. But it wasn't especially interesting. "How could things have gone differently, and turned out better?" I found myself thinking, like some half-baked executive. More than sadness, what welled up in me was the vexed feeling of facing an unsolvable problem.

Outsiders and critics can say whatever they please, but who could really know where, and how, and what might have led to what other outcome? Successes and unmistakable failures, all tangled together, winding their way to this point. Over the years there must have been countless earnest people in charge, countless clever strategists, cycling in and out.

And beyond that, I can't even say whether this "closing" on September 30th is truly a sad thing at all. I'm in no position to pretend I understand. At some point in the nineteenth century the department store was born, changed with the times, grew larger, and has come down to us in its present form. Even if department stores gradually change and eventually disappear, the fact that "people found joy in them" surely won't vanish. The joy of the people who gathered there, that was there, might it not have shifted somewhere else, into some other form, and be shining there still, even if not in the shape of a department store? I turn these things over in my mind, but honestly I don't really understand any of it. I find myself imagining, of all things, our own "Life's Little Pleasures" exhibition, but then again...

◆Today's question, no. 047: "What's something you're glad you bought?" Give it some thought, and if you'd like, write it in an email and send it my way.

Thank you, as always, for coming to Hobonichi today.

I think "the form a store takes" is itself one of the great inventions of an era.
entry.summary: The author visits a closing department store and reflects on the impossibility of understanding why institutions rise and fall, ultimately recognizing that while physical spaces may disappear, the human joy and connection they facilitated endures in other forms.

entry.title: Just write today, no matter what, a little at a time.
entry.content:
I got into an elevator with my daughter, and with her daughter too, meaning my granddaughter. At the back of the elevator, straight ahead, there was a mirror. My seven-year-old granddaughter pulled a funny face at it. My daughter watched and laughed along with her. But I wasn't in the mirror at all. Where on earth was I?

They call it Silver Week, but did such a thing ever exist in the old days? I knew about Golden Week, but did they set this one up in autumn just to rival it? There was already the "Respect for the Aged Day," so maybe they lumped everything around there together under the banner of "silver"? I won't look it up. I've fallen into this habit of checking every little thing, and knowing the "supposedly correct information" about everything has stopped being much fun. Maybe I'll just decide it doesn't exist at all. Silver Week is a lie. There's no such thing.

Language is a convenient thing. Give it a subject and a predicate, and anything at all can be made to stand. He is fleet of foot. A little while ago he ran at three thousand kilometers an hour. The sneakers he was wearing at the time are right here. The soles have worn down considerably from the friction heat. I'll hand these sneakers over to anyone who wants them. I bought them for two hundred yen, so fifty thousand will do. Whether it's true or not, as long as it's grammatically sound, you can spin the whole tale as if it were gospel.

Every day, I've made a habit of "copying Chiikawa" as calligraphy practice. How did the lines that were drawn come to be? When you practice by copying, you naturally start to imagine it. Perhaps, even more than the act of drawing with a brush in hand, imagining what happened during the time the thing was drawn is the more important part.

◆Question no. 46 is "Please tell me a lie." If you're willing, do write one in an email and send it my way.

Thank you for coming to Hobonichi again today. It's perfectly fine, you know, to write a little freely, like dancing however you please.
entry.summary: The essay explores how language, memory, and imagination allow us to construct and reshape reality—from the narrator's absent reflection to invented holidays to tall tales told with perfect grammar—suggesting that truth is less fixed than our willingness to question or reimagine it.

entry.title: The Hobonichi in the station is a little different.
entry.content:
A "Hobonichi Techo Store" has opened inside Tokyo Station. When I say "inside," I mean within the station itself, which means you pass through the ticket gates to get to it. Having a shop of our own "inside a station" was something I (personally) had never even imagined. The plans had been in motion for quite a while, and now, at last, it's open.

My apologies, but until September 19th (Saturday), entry is by lottery reservation only, and from the following day it opens as an ordinary shop. It is inside a station, after all. The hours are long, from ten in the morning until nine at night. And why is that? Again, because it's inside a station.

There really is something special about being inside Tokyo Station. The staff rotations must be quite different from an ordinary workplace, I found myself saying, chatting away like the complete amateur I am. And then something else occurred to me. "Come to think of it, what happens during summer holidays, or New Year's?" I blurted out, rather absentmindedly.

"There aren't any. It's Tokyo Station." The answer came back at once. I could understand the logic well enough, but it struck me that this was the first workplace I'd ever heard of like it. Of course, no single person works there all year round. Even so, the "place" itself never rests. That's what makes it different from an ordinary shop. Yes, yes, I understand, individuals get their days off, properly arranged. Railways and police forces surely operate the same way.

Still, the idea of maintaining a "place that never closes" was something I'd never been able to picture before. "Wow, so that's what they've been doing. What a noble thing," I said, once again sounding like a schoolchild fresh off a social studies field trip.

And then they said it to me. "Itoi-san, you've been running completely every single day yourself, haven't you?" For more than twenty-eight years, it's true, I've kept writing this, day after day.

◆Now then, question no. 45: "Is there something you've kept up for a long time?" I wonder if there is. Please write to us and send your answers by email.

Thank you, as always, for coming to Hobonichi today. They do say that once anything becomes a "habit," you find you can do it.
entry.summary: The opening of a Hobonichi Techo Store inside Tokyo Station—a place that never closes—prompts the author to reflect on the remarkable discipline of maintaining something continuously, a realization that mirrors his own twenty-eight years of daily writing. The essay celebrates the quiet nobility of showing up, day after day, whether as a station or as a writer.

entry.title: Is there motivation, or was there ever any?
entry.content:
Yesterday I wrote, "What on earth is mental strength, anyway?" I simply put down, as it was, the fact that I don't really understand it. But I did notice one thing: that "mental strength" is less something you seek for yourself and more something others demand of you, the fans, the supporters and all the rest.

Today I want to write a little about "desire." It's probably a much bigger theme than I can handle, but I thought I'd write about the word "desire" that has stuck with me ever since childhood.

Once, within earshot of me, some grown-ups were talking. "Once this kid," meaning me, "develops some desire, he'll really grow." In other words, I was regarded as someone who had no "desire." They spoke about it hopefully, as in, "It'll come to him eventually."

What was that "desire" they meant? As for whether any "desire" ever emerged in me after I overheard that, well, it seems it never did.

What the grown-ups were calling "desire" in that moment was, I think now, closer to "drive," or the will to strive.

To be honest, when I sense that kind of drive in other people, I think, "How wonderful." And yet I can hardly ever find that drive in myself. It's not that I lack energy. I'm perfectly lively. It's just that I have no real sense of possessing any "drive." Do I ever put on a performance of "drive"? Maybe a little. Actually, not even that much. Perhaps just a touch.

The boy who, back in elementary school, was supposed to grow stronger "once desire came to him," is he still, even now, unable to summon it? Perhaps, just like "mental strength," "desire," or drive, isn't something that wells up from within you after all.

No, I do want to eat things, I do want to do things. But that feels like something different from "drive," somehow.

◆Question no. 044: "What's the one phrase you've never forgotten?" It can be from any time in your life. If you're willing, please send it in by email.

Thank you for coming to Hobonichi today. The "words" people say really do leave their traces in the most unexpected places.
entry.summary: The author reflects on a childhood comment labeling them as lacking "desire," exploring how this external judgment shaped their understanding of drive and ambition, ultimately questioning whether such qualities are genuinely internal or imposed by others' expectations.

entry.title: What is willpower, anyway?
entry.content:
"In the end, it all comes down to mental strength," you often hear. It's the sort of thing people say about sports, mostly. But what mental strength actually means, I've never really understood. They tell you to stay focused, to keep the tension up, and yet sometimes tension is exactly what makes you stiff, what keeps you from performing at your best. So then, should you just relax? Well, if you're too relaxed, maybe you lose that burst of explosive power. I don't know. For someone like me, it's a mystery.

Generally speaking, in the world of top-level players, where abilities are more or less evenly matched, a tiny difference is what produces a big gap in the results. But in most competitions, the field is a mix of people with genuinely different levels of skill. It might come down to mental strength, sure, but often there's already a real gap in ability before you even get to that.

I've spoken with people who've made their careers as professionals in the sports world, heard all sorts of stories, and when these pro athletes talk about the truly legendary figures among them, they often put it this way: "I completely lost every ounce of confidence I'd had." One of them told me, "The gap in ability between the very best players is wider than the gap between an amateur and a pro." How terrifying is that, really.

Right, mental strength. That's what I was talking about. The idea that sheer willpower can carry you through is an old one. And not just old, I suspect it's actually wrong. But here's the thing about this word, or rather this concept, of mental strength: it's almost always the fans, the supporters, the people who aren't actually out there doing it, who bring it up. If the person actually in the fight says "this will come down to mental strength," then it becomes something more actionable, something closer to science, than mere "mental strength."

People who aren't the ones competing shouldn't be so quick to insist that someone "lacks mental strength." That's what I've come to believe.

◆ Question no. 043: "Has there ever been a time you truly went head-to-head with something?" What do you think? Give it some thought, and if you'd like, write to us by email.

Thank you, as always, for coming to Hobonichi today. Plenty of fans have a rather condescending attitude, don't they. It's tough being an athlete.
entry.summary: The essay challenges the popular notion that "mental strength" alone determines athletic success, arguing that actual ability gaps matter far more and that outsiders who invoke mental strength often misunderstand what elite competitors actually face.

entry.title: There's this thing called the Hobonichi dojo.
entry.content:
A few years back, we started up a "dojo" at Hobonichi. It's not as though we've taken up judo or kendo or anything like that. Though, well, I am practicing tug-of-war pretty hard at the moment.

The "dojo" is a place where you throw around opinions and ideas, where you get thrown and knocked down yourself. Regardless of age or job or career, you toss out all sorts of themes and just talk. It's a bit like free sparring, I suppose. You grapple, no matter what. The senior people aren't necessarily the more skilled ones, but it's also a time when the newcomers get to be present, watching people with a certain amount of experience throw each other around. What matters, above all, is sharing your thoughts and questions.

I once heard that if you ask why the powerhouse teams in sports are so strong, it comes down to the environment of "always being surrounded by strong people," and that this is what nurtures everyone there.

You take a problem that has no easy answer, and each of you turns it over, this way and that, saying maybe it's this, maybe it's that. You think it through in front of everyone, talk it out, and share it. It's perfectly fine for it to have nothing to do with work. Naive things, childish things, likes and dislikes, strange things, we deliberately draw more and more of those elements in.

Painting in broad strokes, maybe the motivation behind all this is "I want to do interesting work." Ah, or perhaps "I want to become an interesting person" fits it better. And not just "interesting" in the comedy sense, mind you. If we made that a theme in the dojo, the conversation might just wander off toward something like, "Isn't there such a thing as boring but interesting?"

Yesterday was a Monday, one of our "dojo" days, and we even had AI join us. We had a good time. It's something we do every week, but for me, the "dojo" has truly become a "dojo" in the real sense.

◆ Today's question, no. 042: "Do you like yourself?" I wonder about that one. It seems simple, and yet difficult... Give it some thought, and if you feel like it, write it in an email and send it my way.

Thank you, as always, for coming to Hobonichi today. "Sharing" is important beyond all reason. The place, and the sharing.
entry.summary: Hobonichi created a "dojo"—a weekly space where employees of all levels freely exchange ideas and grapple with difficult questions together—as a way to build an environment that nurtures interesting thinking and personal growth through shared intellectual exploration. By deliberately including naive, personal, and unconventional perspectives alongside work-related topics, they've discovered that this culture of collaborative problem-solving cultivates both interesting work and interesting people.

entry.title: This is the fun part.
entry.content:
Surprise and familiarity. It seems we're drawn to things that have both.

Not the things we can more or less see coming, but the ones that make us wonder, where did this come from? or, why on earth is this happening? The kind of thing that catches us off guard. In short, surprise.

When something follows a clear, logical progression, this leads to that, and then you get this, there's no real fun in it. But then, hmm, how should I put it, there's this quality of familiarity, a sense that the thing settles in comfortably beside you. It surprises you, yes, but you can tell it isn't your enemy. And before you've even started to like it, some warmth of affection is already drifting your way from its direction. This part matters just as much.

Surprise and familiarity might seem a little contradictory, but there are countless things that manage to hold both at once. Think back on the things you love, the people you love, the things you like to do. Try calling all sorts of them to mind.

With only surprise, you could say it becomes a bit frightening. A little suspense is fine, but too much of it makes you want to keep your distance, I think. And with only familiarity, the joy inevitably fades. It won't necessarily bore you, but you find yourself wanting more play in it, if that makes sense.

Everyone has their own tastes and quirks and chemistry, so I can't say there's one universally good answer. Still, there really are things that make a great many people feel that mix of surprise and familiarity.

Well, as you all know, these days I've been thinking quite a lot about Chiikawa, haven't I? And that world is built from a mountain's worth of surprise and an ocean's worth of familiarity.

◆Question no. 041: "Is there something you're looking forward to?" I think I'll sit with this one and reflect on it myself. If you'd like, please write it down in an email and send it my way.

Thank you, as always, for coming to Hobonichi today.

The thing about AI is that it's missing exactly this, that sense of surprise and familiarity.
entry.summary: People are drawn to things that combine surprise—an unexpected quality that delights—with familiarity—a comforting sense of belonging—and this balance is what makes experiences, people, and creative works truly beloved. Too much surprise alone feels threatening, while familiarity without surprise becomes dull, but the rare things that achieve both create a unique warmth that resonates across different tastes.

entry.title: Just back from a trip and writing in good spirits.
entry.content:
I went to Kyoto for the first time in a while. My schedule happened to have a little room in it, so I managed to drop by two of the places I know well. Of course, part of it is wanting to eat this dish or that dish, but it's also about stopping in, sitting down to a meal, exchanging a few words (not always just a few) with the people who run the place, and confirming that the door at the entrance, the counter, the little wooden menu tags are all just as they used to be, remembering, ah, yes, it was always like this. It's that whole experience I go there for. And when I show my face and they're glad to see me, well, that alone fills me with an absurd amount of happiness.

Let me think, in Kyoto there turned out to be several places I want to visit in that way. One of them was an okonomiyaki restaurant, but it's closed down now, so I can't go anymore. Maybe I could count the croquette shop the butcher runs, too. As I expected, they're all places from the period when I was going to Kyoto frequently. Come to think of it, the only towns with places like that for me are Kyoto and Kesennuma. It's a bit of a shame I can't think of anywhere like that in Maebashi, but, ah, there's the Harashimaya for grilled manju, isn't there.

The real reason for the trip, I suppose it was a project organized by one of Kyoto's universities, was my job taking part in a "three-way talk" up at that spot at Kiyomizu Temple. That was thoroughly enjoyable in its own right, but as a kind of bonus I got to stop by those familiar shops, and I was also lucky that the "Ryokan" exhibition at the Hosomi Museum happened to open this very Saturday, so I could go see it.

I love it, you know, Ryokan's calligraphy. Not "it's good" or anything like that. "I love it" is what fits best. Following the way the characters on display are written with my eyes, imagining it, something wells up in me. It surprised me, too, that Kitaoji Rosanjin, who always struck me as such a sharp-tongued man, praised Ryokan's writing to the skies.

And so, back in Tokyo, the first thing I did was some "Chiikawa calligraphy practice."

◆Today, let's go straight to no. 040, "Do you have a place you go to regularly?" If something comes to mind, send it in by email, why don't you. Thanks in advance.

Thank you again today for coming to Hobonichi. There are several places in Tokyo I go to regularly. I suppose it really is home.
entry.summary: Revisiting cherished familiar places—whether beloved restaurants in Kyoto or regular haunts in Tokyo—offers a profound joy that comes not just from the food or setting, but from the human connection and continuity of returning to spaces that remain comfortingly unchanged.

entry.title: Enjoying the joys of a hot spring in your own bath?
entry.content:
I sink slowly into the bath at home, thinking, ah, there's nothing like a good soak, and yet I find myself wondering why on earth this isn't the same as a hot spring. Lately I've been adding "Kuma's Recommended Hot Spring Essence," made from refined mineral bath salts, so the water I'm soaking in feels awfully close to the real thing. I've even set the temperature a touch on the hot side, going by my memories of actual hot springs. If you consider only the relationship between my body and the water, I really do think this is the same as a hot spring.

You know how, a little while after you've been to a hot spring, you notice, oh, my body's still warm and toasty? I think you really are warmed through, right down inside. And with a bath at home, the kind with the spring essence added, you get something pretty close to that same afterglow. Then there's that feeling while you're actually soaking in the spring water, that sense of, mmm, this is warming me right up, the hot spring is seeping into me. I feel that at home too, in the bath with the essence in it. At this point I'd really like to say they're the same thing.

I'd love to, but the truth is a real hot spring is still better! The bathroom at home looks exactly like the bathroom at home. No matter how expensive the tiles you line it with, it's the family bathroom. There's a real difference between that and stepping into a genuine hot spring where the whole "now this is a hot spring" scenery spreads out before your eyes.

So how could I possibly capture the feeling of a hot spring at home? I kept turning this over in my mind, staring at the dull tiled wall of my own bathroom, and recently I reached a conclusion. What if I simply practiced "getting into the right frame of mind"? If, with my eyes closed, I can convince myself, this is a hot spring, ahhh, this feels wonderful, then it already is a hot spring. And if I can't quite convince myself, well, I'll just keep practicing until I can! That way, I should be able to savor the joy of a hot spring at home every single day. Being the fellow who's lately made a point of "cultivating his subjectivity," I shall surely succeed in luring a hot spring here, free of charge and requiring no equipment whatsoever.

◆Today's Question no.039: "Are you busy?" Simple, isn't it? Give it some thought, and if you like, write it down in an email and send it my way.

Thank you, as always, for coming to Hobonichi today.

A subjective hot spring, which seems a fair bit easier than "quiet the mind and even fire feels cool."
entry.summary: The author discovers that while a home bath with mineral salts can replicate the physical sensation of a hot spring, only by cultivating the right mental state—convincing oneself through imagination—can one truly recreate the complete experience of visiting a real hot spring.

entry.title: More on the karaoke approach to calligraphy copying
entry.content:
I wrote before that karaoke might be a kind of "copying from a master's calligraphy," and honestly, it really is. When you're not just listening but tracing the song with your own voice, singing it, things you never noticed before start to catch your attention.

The same thing happened with "Melody" by Koji Tamaki, a song I love, and so do my karaoke friends. It opens like this: "In this town where you were, the one I loved so much, that song I still love so much, I can still hear it now." And right there, a little uncertainty creeps in.

What was it that was "loved so much," the "you," or "this town"? Then it goes on, "that song I still love so much, I can still hear it now," and this second "love," I think, is probably about "that song." Two "loves," and a "you," a "town," and a "song." You can sing it happily enough without thinking too hard about what modifies what, but the moment you start interrogating it, you lose the thread.

I feel the same way about Mariya Takeuchi's "Eki." There's a line, "that I was the only one who loved," and I'm never quite sure what emotion I'm supposed to sing it with. Two years after the breakup, she happens to catch sight of her old lover. Did she realize "I was the only one who loved him, one-sidedly"? Or did she realize "back then, he loved only me"? The line can be read either way.

With both "Melody" and "Eki," I imagine that for the person who wrote them, it's something they could explain without a second thought: "Oh, it means this." But I think the students doing their "calligraphy copying" through karaoke start to want to sing, in their own voices, whatever it was that was being sung in the "model text."

For what it's worth, as the apprentice loitering at the temple gate, doing my own "copying," I leave both songs "unresolved." Because I think that vagueness is part of what makes a song good.

◆Today is no. 038: "Is there something you've left unresolved?" What might it be? If you'd like, write it in an email and send it our way.

Thank you, as always, for coming to Hobonichi today. Rushing to the right answer isn't always the best thing, is it.
entry.summary: Karaoke, like copying a master's calligraphy, reveals the ambiguities and unresolved emotions embedded in songs, and embracing this vagueness rather than rushing to a single "correct" interpretation is what makes a song truly meaningful.

entry.title: It's not that I don't think about happiness.
entry.content:
Happiness, unhappiness, these aren't things you can speak of easily. I can't even claim to understand my own. To actually say the words out loud, "Ah, I'm so happy," well, that's the sort of thing that only happens in the Kayama Yuzo songs of a certain era, isn't it? No, no, you're allowed to say it, please, say it as much as you like. That's all fine. But there's a theory that goes, "People who are inside happiness don't stop to think about whether they're happy or not," and I remember feeling somehow convinced by it. When someone makes a special point of saying, "I'm happy right now," it feels to me like they're comparing it against something else, something that isn't happiness at all.

If you asked a child playing in the park, gloriously absorbed in nothing, "Are you happy right now?" they might answer "Happy!" without a second thought, but I doubt the idea had even crossed their mind.

The truth is, happiness and unhappiness are a kind of abstract "measuring stick" for how we feel, and people go on living without ever reaching for that stick. Whether a doorway is eighty centimeters wide, or ninety, you'd never think about it in the ordinary course of your life. It's only when it becomes relevant that you start thinking about doors in numbers, "All right, let's go with eighty centimeters." For most of the time we're alive, people should be able to get by without measuring or verifying their happiness. To put it the other way around, it's precisely because we drag out that "measuring stick" of happiness that we end up meeting its flip side, "unhappiness."

And yet, thinking about what happiness actually is, about what constitutes unhappiness and how to escape it, human history has gone on pondering these questions the whole way through. And to be honest, I've done my share of pondering too. But the more I think about it, the more tangled it all becomes. To the point where I catch myself wishing the very concept of happiness didn't exist at all.

◆ Today's question no.037: "Rice, bread, or noodles, which do you like best?"

So? Give it some thought, and if you feel like it, drop me an email and let me know.

Thank you again today for coming to Hobonichi.

And you know, the same thing could be said about the word "love."
entry.summary: True happiness exists most fully when we stop measuring it—the act of examining whether we're happy paradoxically creates the unhappiness we're trying to escape, yet humanity remains perpetually caught in this philosophical contradiction.

entry.title: I shall now excuse myself to the restroom.
entry.content:
This year's "Let's Play Baseball" has come to an end. Some years you head home happy, other years you head home swallowing something back. That's just how it goes.

Anyway, on the "radio broadcast" you can only hear inside the ballpark, there was something I really wanted to say, and I wanted the folks at the commentary desk to agree with me too, so I said it.

"There's this unwritten rule that during a broadcast, neither the announcer nor the commentator is allowed to use the bathroom, and most people talk about that suffering as if it were some cherished memory, but isn't that just not right? To put it strongly, isn't it a bit of a disregard for basic human rights? Of course, doing your best to hold out is the proper attitude for a professional, I understand that, but come on, let's just go. If you need to go, then go. Fundamentally, nothing bad is going to happen. Even if a baseball broadcast went ten minutes without its commentator, even if a staff member near the announcer had to step in and read out the necessary information at the mic, that's not some disaster, and it's hardly an inconvenience. Throughout the history of broadcasting, the desperate struggle to hold it in has been told as a touching anecdote or a source of laughs, but here at our happily slapdash broadcast booth today, let's all feel free to go to the bathroom. I'm sure I'll be going myself."

That was the gist of what I wanted to say.

Soh Taguchi, who has mountains of experience as a baseball commentator, laughed and said, "If you actually did that, it'd be unprecedented."

Well, in the end, though, nobody actually went to the bathroom. There was no particular need to go when nobody especially wanted to, so that was perfectly fine, but if a true professional like Taguchi, or Kato from Sports Hochi, someone from that "you must not go" world had actually gone, it might have made a small article in the sports papers. Probably, for people involved in long sports broadcasts, not going to the bathroom out of a sense of duty was a little bit of a touching tale. But those kinds of touching tales don't really move anyone anymore. The players themselves go to the bathroom and then play the game, after all.

◆ Today's question, no. 036: "What are you holding back on?" Give it some thought, write it down, and if you like, send it to us by email.

Thank you again for coming to Hobonichi today. These long movies they make these days, they've got the bathroom problem too, don't they.
entry.summary: The essay challenges the outdated broadcasting tradition of broadcasters refusing bathroom breaks as a matter of professional pride, arguing that this unnecessary self-denial serves no real purpose and that normalizing basic human needs would be far more sensible than treating such deprivation as a touching mark of dedication.

entry.title: It's not getting old, it's getting seasoned.
entry.content:
Whether it's a town, a building, a shop, or some much larger landscape, whether it's a team, an organization, a role, or a relationship between people, gradually the "thisness" of the thing soaks in. You know how the broth seeps into the daikon in a pot of oden? It's exactly like that.

A shop that looks like just the sort of place people would love these days, well, ask the right specialist and they'll whip one up in no time. You can get people saying "How lovely!" for a while. But even that "How lovely!" gets grubby and grows old. Before long it becomes a shop that "used to be lovely." And then it might be forgotten, might disappear altogether.

But then there are shops nobody ever calls "lovely," and yet they've been going for thirty years. "The owner's a weird guy," "their potato salad is great," praised in these unremarkable ways, and somehow, thirty years. In a shop like that, the shop's own character has "soaked in."

It's the same with streetscapes, a road that's been there since the Edo period, say. There's something soaked into a place like that. Though when you turn it into nice words like "tradition" or "history," it starts to feel a little off, somehow.

Even a married couple who don't seem all that fond of each other, it might not be splendid, might not be beautiful, but something has soaked into them. A flavor that says, this is us, this pair. There it is.

Business matters too, of course it does. But business on its own can't stand the wait, that "time it takes to soak in." Stylish things, expensive-looking things, they're easy enough to build up and tear down again. But the things that have "soaked in," they can't do without time and something like human sweat.

Well now, Hobonichi hits its thirtieth anniversary two years from now, and I got to thinking, all sorts of good broth has been soaking into it, hasn't it.

◆Today's question, no. 035, let's just make it this one. "Is there anything that has soaked into you?" Hard to answer? Well, never mind. Enjoy taking the time to think it over. And then, if you feel like it, please write it in an email and send it along.

Thank you, as always, for coming to Hobonichi today. The pork miso soup at "Hobo Station AKAGI" is a mix of the well-soaked and the freshly made.
entry.summary: True value and character emerge not from deliberate design but from time and accumulated experience—like broth soaking into daikon, the most meaningful things, whether places, businesses, or relationships, develop their irreplaceable essence through years of human presence rather than stylish construction. The author reflects on Hobonichi's approaching thirtieth anniversary as an example of something that has earned its depth through time and care rather than superficial appeal.
